drapeaux.note: English wording as printed by Deseret News (1988), which quotes Michelangelo describing his position to a friend.

accroche: Four years standing, head tilted back, on a scaffold. As early as the 16th century, though, one biographer imagined him on his back.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1508, Pope Julius II entrusts Michelangelo with decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel: the contract is signed on May 8. Born in 1475, the artist will spend four years on the job, until 1512, an entire work to produce above his own head.

The image that comes up most often is of a man lying on his back, brush stretched toward the vault. It was not born in the movies: as early as the 16th century, the biographer Paolo Giovio imagined him that way. Giorgio Vasari and Ascanio Condivi, by contrast, describe a Michelangelo standing up. The image is wrong.

## Standing, Head Tilted Back

Vasari writes that these frescoes "were done with the greatest discomfort, for he had to stand there working with his head tilted backwards." Michelangelo himself describes his position to a friend: "My beard toward Heaven, I feel the back of my brain upon my neck." Standing, then, arms stretched overhead. Never lying down.

A drawn trace of it may survive. A sheet kept at the Casa Buonarroti in Florence pairs a sonnet addressed to the poet Giovanni da Pistoia with a caricature of Michelangelo painting. Caution is in order: the historian Leonard Barkan points out that nothing proves the drawing shows the work on the vault.

## A Team Effort

The American art historian William E. Wallace spent a year in Italy on a National Endowment for the Humanities grant, and the press reported on his research in 1988. He compiled a list of 13 assistants who worked with Michelangelo on the Sistine Chapel. According to him, an architect friend helped design the scaffold, and a carpenter named Piero Basso built it. Michelangelo hired helpers to grind colors, mix paints, trim and clean brushes, and examining the ceiling from the scaffold reveals, Wallace says, other hands "especially painting in the architecture, decoration and many of the secondary figures." The myth of the solitary painter will last anyway, he adds, because these are "fictions that attempt to grasp a superhuman achievement."

## What the Body Paid

Standing with your head tilted back for four years is anything but comfortable. In the sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia, dated to 1509 or 1510, Michelangelo describes what he endures: his beard points at heaven like a finger, his skull scrapes near the back of his neck, his belly is tugged under his chin, and he is bent like a bow (translation by John Frederick Nims, Harvard Magazine). He ends by saying he is no painter.

In 1510, he begins to need to hold his documents at eye level in order to read them. The trouble disappears a few months after the work ends. Researchers proposed in 2012 that it was an acquired, transitory nystagmus caused by the long hours spent looking up.

The myth of the painter lying down is therefore not just an error of detail. It replaces a grueling physical performance, carried out standing, with the help of a team, by a solitary, motionless feat, easier to picture, but one that erases what Michelangelo himself describes: a body bending under the weight of the work.

carte.punch: We picture him on his back. He painted standing, head tilted back.
carte.idee: The myth says Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel lying on his back. Vasari and Condivi describe him standing, and he himself writes of his beard toward Heaven and his head tilted back.

quiz.question: What do we rely on to say that Michelangelo painted standing up rather than lying on his back?
choix: A contract found in the Vatican describes the posture imposed on the artist
His biographers Vasari and Condivi, who describe him working standing up
No painter of the time could have held a brush effectively while lying down
Chemical traces in the fresco show drips that are incompatible with a lying position
quiz.explication: Vasari and Condivi describe Michelangelo standing, and Vasari adds that he worked with his head tilted backwards; Michelangelo himself writes of his beard toward Heaven. Only Paolo Giovio imagined him lying down. No contract or chemical analysis is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to William E. Wallace, how many assistants helped Michelangelo on the Sistine Chapel project?
choix: None: he worked entirely alone on the project
Two apprentices, only in charge of grinding the colors
A team of some 13 assistants, handling a variety of tasks
About 50 workers, as on a construction site
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wallace compiled a list of 13 assistants who worked with Michelangelo on the Sistine Chapel: they ground colors, mixed paints, trimmed and cleaned brushes, and their hands show in the painted architecture, the decoration and many secondary figures.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what happened to Michelangelo's eyesight starting in 1510?
choix: He had to hold his documents at eye level in order to read them
He went completely blind until the end of the project
He developed a cataract that required surgery
His vision improved after years spent with his head tilted up
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1510, Michelangelo has to hold his documents at eye level to read them; the trouble disappears a few months after the work ends, and researchers proposed in 2012 that it was a transitory nystagmus caused by looking up.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, who imagined Michelangelo painting lying on his back?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vasari and Condivi describe Michelangelo standing; it was another biographer, Paolo Giovio, who imagined him on his back.
